personalization_line: the Sean Collier Memorial is one of the projects I keep coming back to — the geometry settles into the site in a way that gets harder to do well, not easier, with time.
the Public Architecture writing has been useful for me — I keep finding myself recommending the section on civic responsibility to people outside the profession.
the Roxbury work has been on my mind — treating affordable housing as a civic project rather than a procurement deliverable is a different argument than most firms even attempt.

Merge's adaptive-reuse projects have stayed with me — there's a sensibility of treating the existing envelope as a found constraint rather than a problem to redesign through, and it's not as common as it should be.
the Center for Coastal Studies has stayed with me — the cantilever lands on the site without overplaying itself, which is a hard thing to pull off in coastal work.
Imagine Boston 2030 is one of the few civic-strategy docs I've actually read end-to-end — the equity-as-program section reframed how I think about architecture's role at the city scale.
the container work is one of those bodies of practice I keep watching — the language has gotten more precise over time rather than more decorative, which is rarer than people give credit for.
the Times Square work has held up for me as the rare civic intervention where the computational backbone never shows at the experience layer — most projects with that ambition leak the math.
the Stealth Building section has become one of the diagrams I reference when trying to explain mixed-use to people who don't naturally think in section.
the investigative-spatial work is the kind of practice expansion that's made me rethink what architects can be useful for — the human-rights casework especially.

the New Lots Library has stayed with me — the column grid reading as a deliberate response to the burial-ground site rather than a default structural choice is the kind of decision I'd want to ask about.

Living Breakwaters keeps coming up in conversations I'm having about coastal work — the section reading as infrastructure and habitat at the same time is unusual enough that it's still doing real teaching.
Galaxy Digital is something I keep going back to study — pulling the studio's aggregation logic up to a 35,000 sf interior without losing the unit-level precision is a hard scale jump.
the BAM Strong awning has been one of my reference points — the in-house design-to-fabrication pipeline you describe on your site is something I keep wishing more practices would build out.
Prismatic at Art Omi has stuck with me — the way one module ends up doing color, sightlines, and structure at once is the kind of compression I keep wanting to learn from.
the Songpa screen has stayed with me — eight twist types yielding a continuous privacy gradient is the kind of constraint problem I find quietly elegant, especially inside a micro-housing budget.

TREEFORM at Venice has been on my mind — the form-finding work with MIT Digital Structures is something I'd love to ask you about, especially the argument that raw timber outperforms glulam when the geometry is solved for the log.
Bivouac for Models has stayed with me — the doubling at two scales is one of those moves that gets funnier and more interesting the longer I look at it.
Moakley Park has stayed with me — landscape sections that double as flood defense without reading as defensive infrastructure is a category of work I keep coming back to.

the Kendall Square garage screens have stayed with me — wrapping a parking structure to do real public-realm work at that budget is genuinely hard, and most attempts I see fail the budget test or fail the perception test.
the Holocaust Museum's woven stainless mesh is a project I think about often — the metaphor and the geometry support each other without either feeling overdetermined, which is rare in memorial work.
the Fireberry house has stayed with me — the way it reads as a contemporary New England compound without leaning on the typology too heavily is harder than it looks.

Frank — congrats on the AIA fellowship. I keep coming back to your Cambridge additions — the restraint of letting pre-1900 envelopes lead the design conversation rather than fight it is a discipline that doesn't get talked about enough.

the Old Derby Building work in Hingham has been on my mind — additions inside an 1818 shell that the Historical Commission signs off on is a kind of design rigor that doesn't get talked about enough.

the Cambridge Historical Commission preservation awards your team keeps winning are exactly the work I most want to see more of — the discipline of operating inside an existing condition is its own design language.

personalization_line: the Ware & Van Brunt townhouse renovation in Back Bay has been on my mind — keeping the brick shell while gutting the interior is the kind of constraint that produces some of the more honest detailing I've seen recently.

Quahaug Point has stayed with me — the offset shed-roof volumes feel like a genuine engagement with Newport vernacular rather than a quotation of it, which is harder to do well than people give credit for.

the body of work inside the Edgartown Historic District is one of those practice arcs I keep watching — building 225 homes inside a single historic district while keeping each one specific is a design-discipline problem, not just a permitting one.

the Cartier Mansion restoration has stayed with me — preserving the Codman spiral stair while replacing every system around it is the kind of project that lives or dies on coordination, and the result reads cleanly.
the Washington Square pied-à-terre has been on my mind — curved partitions in a 1,400 sf footprint is the kind of small-scale spatial move that requires a lot of iteration to get right.
the Hidden Hollow project has stayed with me — the way the section opens to landscape without becoming a glass box is a hard thing to pull off in custom residential at that scale.

the Carroll Gardens townhouse has been on my mind — keeping the period front intact while reworking the rear through a single stair move is the kind of strategic restraint I keep wishing more renovations attempted.
the Park Slope row house featured in Brownstoner last fall has stayed with me — the not-quite-gut approach to a brownstone reno is a much harder design call than going either direction fully.

the Clinton Hill townhouse conversion has been on my mind — pulling a multifamily back to a single-family while carving out a garden apartment is a kind of typological negotiation that doesn't always work, and yours did.

the Little Monster Films HQ has stayed with me — fitting a film-production company into a Flatiron loft without making it feel staged is harder than it looks, and the millwork is doing a lot of work quietly.
the Aperture Foundation HQ has been on my mind — institutional fit-outs that read more like residential than corporate is a sensibility I keep watching for.
the residential work at 7 West 57th has stayed with me — minimalist envelopes with that level of joinery detail is the kind of approach that requires real conviction to keep clean.
